description: I built a homelab agent control plane. Most of it is running. The product is not a chatbot with root. The product is the contracts: who may write what, where truth lives, which mod
text:
I built a homelab agent control plane. Most of it is running. The product is not a chatbot with root. The product is the contracts: who may write what, where truth lives, which models may see which data, and how a bad merge is undone.

One human. Two hats.

The builder hat sits in the IDE. That is where I author GitOps, policy, the model front door, and the tool registry. Unattended agents do not rewrite those contracts.

The operator hat sits in a self-hosted run console. Missions start there. Specialists report back. Run agents open merge requests. The shared inbox is git. A reconciler applies the default branch. The cluster is disposable. Git, secrets, DNS, and the CA are not.

Agents split the work:
- The orchestrator classifies BUILD versus RUN and dispatches.
- Sub-agents stay on local or self-hosted models, use read tools, and return structured findings. They do not comment, open MRs, or call write tools. Public cloud is denied for them.
- Run agents may mutate after policy allow: desired-state MRs, lab-guest snapshot or start or stop, write tools through one gateway. A human still merges main. Rollback is git revert.

The board in git (image) is the shape:

- Local inference first. One LLM proxy. Policy on every class. A dedicated GPU guest for chat and embeddings. Self-hosted overflow next. Public cloud last, vault token, never for sub-agents.
- Observability in the design, not after. Host logs into Splunk. Traces and metrics off the cluster. Spend and GPU views on the house dashboards.
- Security by construction. One secret store. One tool gateway, no raw MCP URLs. Short-lived SSH certs. Name-limited CA. Default deny. Writes stay on the run role.

Still dropping dual-write of workload secrets. The shape is the point.

title: Every AI agent in my home lab used to share one login. Network, security, monitoring, self-hosting — five…
description: Every AI agent in my home lab used to share one login. Network, security, monitoring, self-hosting — five different jobs, one shared key, full access to everything, all the time. T
text:
Every AI agent in my home lab used to share one login. Network, security, monitoring, self-hosting — five different jobs, one shared key, full access to everything, all the time.

This week each one got its own identity instead. Not a longer-lived version of the same shared secret — a distinct, narrowly-scoped credential per agent, so each one can reach exactly what its job needs and structurally nothing else.

Then the same pattern turned up somewhere I didn't expect it. I'd built a small tool so my agents can post updates like this one — and the easy version of that tool hands every agent a live token to my professional accounts. I didn't want that sitting in five different places, so the tool holds the real credential exactly once. Every agent gets a scoped key to the tool itself, never to the platform, and the one action that actually goes public needs a confirmation step no agent can trigger alone. This post went through that exact gate.

None of it counted until I watched it work. I authenticated as the narrow identity directly and confirmed it could reach what it should — and genuinely couldn't reach what it shouldn't. Then I proved it again with a real agent making a real call, watching the response come back for real.

Non-human identity isn't something you tick off once and move on. It's only real the day you've actually watched it refuse the wrong thing.

If your agents still share one login today — what would it actually cost you the day one of them goes wrong?

title: I gave each of my AI agents a different brain this week. Then I watched one nearly fall asleep mid-task.
description: I gave each of my AI agents a different brain this week. Then I watched one nearly fall asleep mid-task. In my homelab I run a small fleet of agents through one gateway. Until now
text:
I gave each of my AI agents a different brain this week. Then I watched one nearly fall asleep mid-task.

In my homelab I run a small fleet of agents through one gateway. Until now they all shared a single model. This week I routed each agent to the model that fits its job, and instead of buying a bigger GPU, I securely connected to a friend's GPU across the internet.

The orchestrator ("CEO") runs a 120B open model on friend 1's AI host. The two heavy infra agents run on Friend 2's hosted model. Everyone else stays on my local GPU. Call it #meshAI: when you can't afford more silicon, ask a mate. Wire it together over a VPN, and your "cluster" suddenly spans three houses.

The switch itself was beautiful: one field per agent, no redeploys, instantly reversible. So I fired a real task, a quick substrate health briefing, and let the CEO delegate.

Back came one consolidated report: a service-health table from the infra agent (cluster services all active), 11 active VLANs from the network agent, and a clean error scan from observability. One ask in, three brains on three models across three houses, one answer out.

Then the messy bit: that 120B model is 65GB. Cold, the first call took five minutes instead of ninety seconds, long enough that my own watchdog declared the run "stranded" and tried to recover something that was simply still loading.

The lesson: per-agent routing is the easy part. Model readiness is the hard part.

Options I'm weighing: keep the big model warm with a heartbeat, raise the stranded-run timeout, or give the orchestrator a smaller, faster brain and save the heavyweight for the work that needs it.

Right model for the right job, borrowed from the right mate. Including the job of waking up.

title: Most "AI memory" problems aren't storage problems. They're filing problems.
description: Most "AI memory" problems aren't storage problems. They're filing problems. I've been building a multi-agent setup at home where several AI harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, cron jobs
text:
Most "AI memory" problems aren't storage problems. They're filing problems.

I've been building a multi-agent setup at home where several AI harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, cron jobs, autonomous agents) all work on the same system. The obvious question came up fast: where does their memory live?

The tempting answer is "one database, everything goes in." That's the trap.

What actually worked was splitting memory into three stores, each authoritative for a different kind of fact:

Git holds durable, curated truth — the plans, the decisions, the standards. Anything that has to survive, be diffable, and be reviewed before it counts.

An episodic memory API holds session history — what each agent did, decided, and learned this time round, so the next one inherits context instead of starting cold.

Local harness memory is just a private scratchpad. Convenient, but never the source of truth, because no other agent can see it.

The whole design exists to prevent one failure: putting a fact in the wrong store. A decision that belongs in git rotting in a local cache. Session noise polluting the durable record. Each store has one job, and "promote it to the right place" is a first-class rule.

Funnily enough, this is just good filing discipline — the same instinct that keeps a homelab sane — applied to machines that remember.

Curious how others are handling memory across multiple agents. One big store, or a split like this?

title: Recently I wrote about my homelab "substrate" — a board of AI agents running on my own hardware, and why…
description: Recently I wrote about my homelab "substrate" — a board of AI agents running on my own hardware, and why the system around the models matters more than any single model. I mentione
text:
Recently I wrote about my homelab "substrate" — a board of AI agents running on my own hardware, and why the system around the models matters more than any single model. I mentioned, almost in passing, that I'd swapped the model class underneath them. This post is the why, because it's the part I get asked about most: how you actually choose the model.

Here's the thing nobody tells you. Choosing a model is an architecture decision, and you make it BEFORE you go chasing whatever topped the leaderboard this week. Decide the model class first. Then go shopping.

Let me show you why, the hard way.

My agents were running on hybrid reasoning models — the kind that think out loud before they answer. Great on paper. But on my agentic tool-calling path, that internal monologue leaked straight into the output and back into the context window.

So instead of a clean tool call, my agents were posting their own thought process. "Let me check the constraints... I will now post the comment..." The reasoning bloated the context, polluted the structured output, and added latency and token cost on every single hop.

I switched to an instruction-tuned, non-reasoning model — no narration, just the answer. Clean, direct, reliable tool calls. For agentic work, the model that just does the job beat the "smarter" one that narrates it.

Think of it like GDP. Productivity is useful output per unit of input — compute, tokens, latency, and the human cleanup tax. By that measure a reasoning model can win the benchmark and still deliver lower real productivity for your job, because it burns resources thinking aloud and then you pay again to clean it up.

So the decision driver isn't rank. It's three things: the use case, the output shape you actually need (tool-use wants clean deterministic calls, not an essay), and the resources you'll spend — a 16GB Mac is a very different budget to a GPU rig or paid cloud tokens.

Smartest model isn't the same as most productive model for this job on these resources.

How are you choosing: leaderboard rank, or fit for the output you actually need?

description: A while back I posted something deliberately abstract: the idea of an "agentic substrate", a foundation my homelab could run future ideas on. This is that idea taking shape. The vi
text:
A while back I posted something deliberately abstract: the idea of an "agentic substrate", a foundation my homelab could run future ideas on. This is that idea taking shape.

The vision was easy to say and hard to build: agents that don't just chat, but actually operate my infrastructure. I now have a working "board" of them. A CEO agent breaks a request into tasks and delegates to a council of specialist "eng-ops" agents covering infra, network, observability and security. They do the work, grounded in real data through Splunk and MCP tools that reach into my network and hosting admin layers.

It runs on Paperclip, which orchestrates the board. But the agents aren't locked inside an app: each persona, its role, instructions and guardrails, lives as a versioned file in a self-hosted GitLab repo. That repo is part of a memory architecture that lets multiple agents, and multiple AI harnesses, work off the same source of truth and review changes like code.

Under the agents sits a control plane I care about as much as the agents. vLLM serves the local model on my RTX 4080 SUPER. LiteLLM is the gateway every call routes through, with an allow-list that decides what can go where. OPA holds per-agent tool grants, so each agent only gets the capabilities it's explicitly allowed.

That governance earns its place. The gateway only routes to destinations on an explicit allow-list, so nothing leaves on-prem by accident. When I sanctioned an external provider (superdupercloud) for the heavier agents, its own secret-aware filter refused the agents that handle credentials. When a new agent reached for my admin layer before its grant was wired up, it got a hard 401.

On models: a 15-model bake-off landed me on IBM's Granite. Clean, non-reasoning, reliable tool calls. But the bigger unlock was refining each agent's prompt. Same model, tighter instructions, completely different reliability.

So I've stopped chasing perfect determinism from the models. I'm building it into the system around them: scoped tools, policy at the gateway, versioned personas, validation at the seams. The substrate is the product, not any single model.

Next is extending tool use and hardening that systems-level determinism, measured against real accuracy and efficiency for my use cases.

Screens below: the council running live on the board, and the local GPU pinned at 100% as the 8B model works.

Do you push for deterministic models, or deterministic systems?

Footnote: this post was written by AI with my coaching and direction. Given the subject, that felt only fair.

text:
SPL has always been Splunk's superpower. The way you wield it just changed.

For years, getting value out of Splunk meant getting fluent in SPL — chaining commands through the pipe, leaning on stats, eval and rex to turn messy machine data into answers. That skill still matters. But the interface to it is being rewritten.

The new Splunk MCP Server (Model Context Protocol) lets an AI agent talk to Splunk in natural language. It explores your data, taps saved searches and lookups, and uses Splunk's AI Assistant to generate, optimise and explain the SPL for you — all inside Splunk's own authentication and role-based access, so the agent only ever sees what you're cleared to see.

Now layer that over the Cisco Data Fabric: machine data federated across edge, cloud and hybrid — Iceberg, Delta Lake, Snowflake, Azure — analysed where it lives instead of dragged into one place. Suddenly you can ask, in plain English, "where are we seeing anomalous auth failures this week?" or "which product lines are trending against last quarter?" and an agent answers across the whole fabric, securely.

That's the real shift: from memorising SPL syntax to asking sharper questions. The fundamentals don't disappear — an agent is only as good as the query behind it — but the modern path is agentic, natural-language, and federated.

Security threats and business insight, from the same conversation. That's the agentic AI era arriving in observability.

text:
Warning: This is a bit abstract. ... I hope you read on. 

🏗️ For ~3 weeks I've been building a family operating system.   

Not "AI for the family" — that's apps + Shortcuts.

Not "smart home" — that's hardware orchestration.

A genuine operating system for running the family + its ventures with the same rigor an enterprise applies to its own substrate.

Charters. Bylaws. Internal audit. Change control. Separation of duties. Reversibility classification. Identity & access management. Source-of-truth.

Five enterprise principles, applied at family scale:

📜 1. Constitutional governance. Every binding rule is a written, ratified, amendable artefact in version control. The system cannot evolve faster than its doctrine. Same shape an enterprise applies to its compliance manual.

🤖 2. AI agents as governed principals (not assistants). Each agent has a binding contract — identity, mandate, authority scope, tool capability matrix with reversibility classes (R1 read-only → R4 irreversible), red lines inherited from foundation guardrails. Same shape an enterprise applies to service accounts + IAM roles.

🧱 3. Structural isolation. Different domains of life run in different "Companies." Cross-domain bleed is prevented at the infrastructure layer, not the prompt layer. Same shape an enterprise applies to subsidiary data isolation + tenant boundaries.

🔍 4. Audit-by-default + reversibility-aware decisions. Every action through chokepoint services emits canonical events. Every destructive operation requires Board pre-approval. Same shape an enterprise applies to change-management gates + SOC 2 controls.

📝 5. Source-controlled change. Every modification is a signed git commit, a ratified amendment, a tagged release. Drift surfaces as an incident. Same shape an enterprise applies to its production substrate.

📊 By the numbers:
• 4 repos · 283 signed commits · 278 tagged releases
• 9 AI agents — each with a binding 5-file contract
• 38 ratification artefacts — every rule has a written amendment trail
• 13 named standards · plan at 3.2K lines / 46K words
• ~71K lines of source-controlled doctrine + code
• ~8,340 LLM turns · ~3B tokens through the build

🎯 The bet: a family-as-enterprise can be operated with the rigor of a regulated business — without the bureaucracy.

Two operators. Multiple ventures. Multiple personas. AI agents staffing the work. Audit trail, approval gates, reversibility classes, persona isolation — all enforced at the substrate layer.

⚖️ Corporate governance machinery + family-as-operating-unit intent. Two things usually treated as opposites. They turn out to compose.
Working name: a constitutionally-governed AI operating system for the family-as-enterprise.

🤝 If you've been thinking about your family/household as something that could be operated rather than just lived in — or wrestling with agent-governance at any scale — I'd love to compare notes.

text:
🧪 I started with a simple goal: learn Splunk data onboarding properly.

Not just “click around Splunk Web and hope it makes sense” learning. I wanted a practical lab where I could see the full journey from data source to searchable event.

So I built a local Docker-based Splunk forwarding lab with agentic help.

It started as a basic setup: Splunk Enterprise, Deployment Server, Heavy Forwarder, Universal Forwarder, some sample logs, and a few lessons.

Then, as usual, the scope grew legs.

The lab now has:
✅ Direct UF -> Indexer forwarding
✅ UF -> HF -> Indexer forwarding
✅ File, TCP, UDP, JSON, XML, HEC, scripted, and masked PII data sources
✅ Dedicated indexes per data source type
✅ A visual topology map
✅ A Lab CLI pane that shows the actual relevant config files for each source
✅ inputs.conf, outputs.conf, props.conf, transforms.conf, serverclass.conf, and deployment apps wired into the flow
✅ Regex masking on the Heavy Forwarder before events are indexed

The most useful part wasn’t just getting it working.

It was iterating through the things that broke: embedded Splunk cookie handling, forwarders not picking up config consistently, stale HEC tokens, index routing mistakes, and figuring out where parsing actually happens.

That’s the bit I wanted from this project: not a demo, but a learning cockpit.

There’s something powerful about making infrastructure visible. When you can click a data source and immediately see the files that make it work, the mental model starts to stick.

Still rough around the edges, but it’s becoming exactly the kind of hands-on lab that suits my learning style.

text:
"Which AI agent should I use?" is the wrong question. The right question is: what are you trying to automate — and at what level? Most people haven't mapped that out yet.

Here's how I think about it: three layers — execution (doing the work), workflow (coordinating the work), and governance (managing who does what, at what cost, with what guardrails). Different tools, different jobs.

Execution layer: Cursor, Claude Code, Codex CLI. Cursor gives you an AI-first editor with tight inline integration. Claude Code goes deeper — full codebase context, end-to-end task execution, terminal-native. Codex CLI is OpenAI's answer to the same problem. I run Claude Code and Cursor daily; they complement more than they compete. Codex is worth watching if you're deeper in the OpenAI ecosystem.

Workflow layer: Claude CoWork and OpenClaw. CoWork takes the same agentic engine as Claude Code and points it at knowledge work — non-developers, local files, multi-step tasks outside a code editor. OpenClaw is broader: a 24/7 agent workforce across 200+ models, email, calendar, Slack, browser. Not a dev tool — an automation platform. Different job, different configuration discipline.

Governance layer: Paperclip (and LangGraph). This is where it gets interesting. LangGraph gives developers graph-based control over multi-agent pipelines — powerful, but you're writing the plumbing. Paperclip takes a different bet: org charts, budgets, approval gates, configured not coded. Enterprise platforms like UiPath and watsonx have done this for years — Paperclip just made it accessible. 30K GitHub stars in three weeks suggests the timing is right.

This is my mental model of the space right now. What am I not considering?

What actually makes a good AI agent?

Not just a working one. A *good* one.

I started where most people do — structured context (md files, system prompts) that gives an agent its identity and purpose, combined with a model's reasoning capability. Add tooling and you have something that can act on the world.

I've been building a system around those three layers — Identity, Cognition, and Action — and it's starting to feel solid.

But lately my thinking has shifted.

Because once you have agents that work, new questions emerge:

→ How do you manage memory and state across runs?
→ How do you know when an agent is drifting from its purpose?
→ How do you maintain visibility into what it's actually doing?
→ And maybe most practically — how do you avoid agent bloat as your ecosystem grows?

That last one is where my head is right now. It's easy to keep adding agents. Much harder to know when to consolidate, retire, or redesign one.

I don't have the answers yet. But I think the lifecycle question is just as important as the build question.

text:
I gave Claude Code a live Splunk lab and said "figure out why queries hang."

It traced the issue end-to-end: Docker logs → MCP server source → the upstream GitHub repo. The root cause? A single McpServer instance shared across all SSE connections. Every new client connect() call invalidates every other active session — so two concurrent clients (Claude Code + the lab's chat service) just keep killing each other in a loop.

Claude didn't just find it. It forked the repo, wrote the fix, pushed the branch, drafted the PR description, rebuilt the Docker image from the patched branch, and validated the fix by querying the live Splunk instance.

The whole thing — diagnosis, code fix, PR, rebuild, test — one conversation.

What struck me most: it reasoned through MCP SDK internals, identified a race condition in someone else's code, and proposed a minimal correct fix without being pointed at the right files. That's not autocomplete. That's a debugging partner.

The lab itself is open source — a self-contained Splunk + MCP environment for experimenting with AI-powered observability workflows. If that's your kind of thing, come follow along or contribute.

title: Do you actually know what Claude has access to on your machine?
description: Do you actually know what Claude has access to on your machine? I didn't. Not fully. I'd been clicking "yes" to tool approvals — filesystem reads, bash commands, API calls — withou
text:
Do you actually know what Claude has access to on your machine?

I didn't. Not fully. I'd been clicking "yes" to tool approvals — filesystem reads, bash commands, API calls — without a complete picture of what was accumulating across tokens, MCP servers, and OAuth integrations.

So I built a /security-audit skill for Claude Code. On demand, it:

- Validates every API token live (LinkedIn, GitHub PAT, HuggingFace, Splunk, Webex)
- Audits the filesystem MCP root — lists every repo Claude can read or write
- Checks Claude Code's permission rules (allow/deny) for overly broad grants
- Scans for .env files, private keys, and credentials sitting in the accessible path
- Assesses blast radius: if something went wrong, what could actually be touched?

The first run surfaced some real stuff. Live credentials for Proxmox, Cloudflare, and GitLab in repos Claude had full read/write access to. A GitHub token registered under a different variable name than what env.sh exported. An old curl command permanently auto-approved in settings.local.json from a debugging session I'd forgotten about.

None of it was catastrophic. But it was exactly the kind of drift that builds quietly when you're moving fast on an MVP.

The skill writes a dated audit report to the repo. Reproducible, reviewable, commitable.

https://lnkd.in/ghpD4Hkg

If you're running Claude Code with MCP servers and local file access, you should know what you've said yes to.

#ClaudeCode #AITools #Homelab #SecurityMindset

text:
You always remember your first MCP server build.

Mine took a day. I had an itch — I needed a way to programmatically manage Cloudflare DNS and tunnel services from Claude Code. No tool existed. So I just went.

I probably should have specced it out more before I started. Instead I went straight to building, which meant a lot of rework, a few architectural pivots, and more troubleshooting than I'd care to admit.

But here's the thing — it works. Thirteen MCP tools, a full CI pipeline with integration tests against a live Cloudflare API, and a clean workflow for exposing SSH and web services through Cloudflare Access in one command. Built it, used it, shipped it.

The lesson isn't "spec more" (though, yes, spec more). It's that the best way to learn a new primitive — MCP, a new API, a new infra pattern — is to have a real problem you actually need to solve. The motivation fills in the gaps your knowledge can't.

text:
35 hours. That's what AI-assisted development handed back to me in a single week.

I built a portable Claude Code resource library from scratch — skills for LinkedIn, Webex, Splunk dashboards, blog publishing, repo auditing. OAuth flows. CI/CD pipelines. Cross-device setup scripts. The kind of project that would normally sit on a backlog for a month because "I'll get to it on the weekend."

Here's the thing: I'm not a developer. Never have been. My background is infrastructure and architecture — I read code better than I write it. But this week, that didn't matter. Every evening, kids in bed, laptop open, shipping code faster than I ever have.

The Splunk dashboard skill alone — connecting to the API, wrangling TLS cert issues, generating AI background images via HuggingFace, deploying live — I'd estimate 8–12 hours of research and trial and error for someone who does this daily. It was a few sessions for me.

I'm not pretending I didn't work hard. But there's a difference between hard work that drags and hard work that moves. And those recovered hours? They went back to the weekend. Football with the kids. Not debugging OAuth.

If the barrier for you has been "I'm not a developer" — it's not the barrier it used to be. The motivation to build something real is enough to get started.

title: Measure twice, cut once. It's a carpenter's rule — but it's the most important thing I've learned building…
description: Measure twice, cut once. It's a carpenter's rule — but it's the most important thing I've learned building with AI. AI can write code fast. Dangerously fast. The trap is skipping t
text:
Measure twice, cut once. It's a carpenter's rule — but it's the most important thing I've learned building with AI.

AI can write code fast. Dangerously fast. The trap is skipping the thinking and letting it rip. I've done it. The result is a technically impressive pile of the wrong thing.

So I built BuilderMate — my personal AIOps operating model. Before a single line of code gets written, every project goes through a structured spec protocol: purpose, three core capabilities, integrations, what's explicitly out of scope, and a definition of done. Then infrastructure tests and application test stubs are written. Only then does implementation begin.

The output is a living blueprint — covering the full pipeline from Linear ticket to CI gates to DNS automation to monitoring. The kind of thing you'd normally only see on enterprise whiteboards, applied to solo side projects.

The image below is one of the artefacts from this week: a full architecture reference for the self-hosted variant of the platform. It's not the code. It's the thinking — and that's the part that makes the code actually worth writing.

With AI in the loop, you can build fast AND build right. But you still have to do the measuring.

text:
One command. Live Splunk dashboard. AI-generated background image. Zero manual clicking.

I built `/splunk-dashboard-gen` — a Claude Code skill that takes a Splunk index, an SPL query, and a title, then does the rest itself.

It runs the query, analyses what kind of data it's looking at (network events? auth logs? IoT telemetry?), synthesises a matching image generation prompt, fires that at a HuggingFace image model, embeds the result as a base64 background, builds the full Dashboard Studio JSON, and deploys it live to Splunk via the REST API.

The screenshot below is a real example — a Sankey flow showing my Meraki MX routers → VLANs → connected devices at home. The background was AI-generated from the data context. The whole thing was deployed from one `/splunk-dashboard-gen` command in Claude Code.

What I found interesting building this: the hardest part wasn't the image gen or the Splunk API. It was getting Claude to write a good image prompt — one dark and ambient enough to sit behind charts without competing with them. Prompt-engineering the prompt engineer is a bit meta, but it works.

title: I've always joked that I work in the "ideas department."
description: I've always joked that I work in the "ideas department." Big concepts, ambitious plans, whiteboards full of architecture. Then reality hits: the gap between idea and working system
text:
I've always joked that I work in the "ideas department."

Big concepts, ambitious plans, whiteboards full of architecture. Then reality hits: the gap between idea and working system is enormous, and there are only so many hours after the kids are in bed.

AI closed that gap for me.

The shift wasn't about automating the boring stuff. It was about learning to give an agent a proper briefing — context, constraints, conventions — then designing the system together rather than just prompting at it.

In the last month that's looked like: a portable AI toolchain synced across every machine I own, MCP servers for Cloudflare and Cisco circuit registries, GitOps pipelines for lab and network config, Splunk on Proxmox, a full Packer → Terraform → Ansible → GitLab CI build chain, and a lifecycle management app for tracking Cisco hardware EOL dates.

A month ago most of those were ideas on a list.

The skill I think matters most right now isn't prompt engineering or AI literacy. It's engineering judgment — knowing how to decompose a concept, brief an agent, and recognise when the output is actually right.

The ideas department finally has a delivery team.

text:
Asked my Splunk Enterprise server a question in Claude Desktop today. Got a live answer back in seconds.

No SPL. No dashboard hunting. Just natural language straight to my Splunk data — inside the same tool I'm already using to write code, plan infrastructure, and reason about problems.

Getting there took some work. Claude Desktop and Claude Code are separate ecosystems with separate configs. Desktop doesn't source your shell profile, so tokens and env vars have to be explicitly passed via the mcpServers block. Throw in a self-signed cert and mcp-remote as a stdio-to-HTTPS bridge, and there's enough moving parts to get wrong.

But once it's wired up? You stop context-switching. You stop writing SPL from memory. You ask a question, you get an answer, you move on.

PwC Consumer Intelligence Series, Trusted Tech Survey, 2020" https://lnkd.in/gcTiDN5P 

When I think about Healthcare, we have to build trust with the workforce as well as the public when it comes to the digital healthcare services that they interact with, otherwise adopton will be slow. Trust comes with positive experiences as well as the ability to respond quickly when a digital service is not working. 

The challenge -  healthcare technology and the information systems landscape is complex, many parts and is on a journey to be more integrated (loosely coupled through API's) for greater value.  Complexity is only going to increase.

To help digest this I've created an infographic that outlines this complexity at a high level and I draw your attention to the red lines.

These red lines will be a combination of services you own (e.g. EMR) and services that your don't (e.g leveraging cloud ML/AI at scale). 

Do you have visibility of those red lines, between them and their dependancies on your digital service? 

Please get in touch if think digital assurance is going to help accelerate or derisk your adoption of digital healthcare services.
